sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: Support multiple people editing one document while seeing each other's changes and cursor positions.
Concurrent editing requires an operation-merging model; transmitting whole snapshots is not enough to prevent lost work.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: Create and load documents.
Apply concurrent edits and show updates in real time.
Display collaborator presence and cursors.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: Keep typing responsive with local feedback and low-latency propagation.
Converge to a consistent document despite concurrent edits, retries, and reconnects.
Persist edits durably and scale connection handling independently from document storage.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: Document stores identity, permissions, and the latest snapshot/version.
Operation records an edit with client identity, operation ID, and ordering or causal metadata.
Session tracks an active collaborator; Presence stores ephemeral cursor and availability information.

sections.title: API
points: Create a document and fetch its snapshot plus synchronization position.
Open an authenticated document collaboration channel and submit operations with stable IDs.
Receive accepted operations and acknowledgements; reconnect from a known revision or synchronize using the chosen merge protocol.
Send presence separately from durable document edits because stale cursor updates can be discarded.

sections.title: 1) Create and load
points: Persist metadata and an initial snapshot, enforcing document access on both HTTP requests and persistent connections.
Load a snapshot and all operations after its position before presenting a fully synchronized document.
Buffer live events during initial loading or use a boundary token so edits are not missed between snapshot and subscription.

flows.title: Load a document and join collaboration
steps: The client requests the document; the service checks read/edit permission before returning state or opening an edit channel.
The synchronization service establishes a snapshot revision and a live-operation boundary, buffering or retaining changes needed during loading.
The client loads the snapshot and applies operations after its revision in the order required by the chosen collaboration model.
It merges buffered live operations and acknowledges the last applied position, avoiding a gap between snapshot loading and subscription.
Presence is registered separately and expires if the session disappears; it is not part of the durable document content.

sections.title: 2) Concurrent editing
points: Whole-document replacement allows one client's stale snapshot to overwrite another client's work.
Operational transformation adjusts incoming operations against concurrent edits, commonly with a server-defined order.
CRDTs encode operations or state so replicas can merge and converge under their defined rules.
Choose one model and explain its metadata, ordering, and storage costs rather than treating the two approaches as interchangeable boxes.
Apply edits locally for responsiveness, then reconcile acknowledgements and remote edits using that model.

flows.title: Apply an edit with a server-ordered OT design
steps: The client applies the user's edit locally for responsiveness and sends an operation ID plus its base revision.
The document owner verifies permission and deduplicates a previously accepted operation with the same ID.
It transforms the operation against intervening accepted operations according to the chosen OT rules and assigns the next authoritative revision.
The server durably appends the accepted operation before acknowledging the durable revision and broadcasting it to collaborators.
Other clients transform or reconcile pending local edits and apply the remote operation; the origin reconciles its acknowledgement instead of applying its own insertion twice.
After disconnecting, a client resumes from its acknowledged revision or a new snapshot. A CRDT-based design uses its causal/merge rules instead of this OT transformation step.

sections.title: 3) Broadcast and presence
points: Route document operations to the collaboration owner or shared document channel and broadcast accepted edits.
Deduplicate operations by ID; reconnect replay must not insert the same text twice.
Cursor positions need transformation or stable anchors as text changes around them.
Expire presence after missed heartbeats; a disconnected collaborator should not remain permanently online.

sections.title: 1) Connection scaling
points: Partition active documents across collaboration servers and route all participants to the appropriate owner or channel.
Separate persistent connection gateways from durable operation storage when needed.
A very popular document remains a hot key; limit or specialize its collaboration path rather than assuming more document shards fix it.
On owner failure, recover from durable state and force clients to resume from acknowledged positions.

sections.title: 2) Bound storage and replay
points: An append-only operation log supports recovery but grows indefinitely and makes cold loads slow.
Periodically create a snapshot at a known log position, then replay only later operations.
Compact safely: retain what offline clients and the merge algorithm still need, including relevant tombstones or revision history.
Publish snapshots atomically with their boundary so readers cannot combine a new snapshot with the wrong operation range.

flows.title: Publish a consistent snapshot
steps: A snapshot worker chooses a committed document revision as its boundary.
It reconstructs or captures the document exactly through that revision and writes the snapshot to durable storage.
It atomically publishes the snapshot reference together with the covered revision after the write succeeds.
New readers load that snapshot and replay only later operations; they do not combine it with an unrelated log boundary.
Compaction removes history only after the retention and synchronization rules permit it, preserving metadata still needed by offline clients or the merge algorithm.

sections.title: Final Design
points: Durable snapshots and an operation log support recovery and history.
A selected OT or CRDT model defines concurrent edit semantics; collaboration servers deliver its operations in real time.
Separate ephemeral presence, bounded replay, and authenticated document routing keep the editing experience responsive and recoverable.
